Newborn litters of the White-tailed antelope squirrel (Ammospermophilus leucurus) typically contain eight pups per litter [N_R_i = eight pups per litter], a fecundity level that is modest compared to many other ground-dwelling sciurids. Females generally produce approximately 1.3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.3 litters per year], which likely represents a trade-off between the energetic demands of lactation and the constraints imposed by a relatively short active season in arid environments. At birth, the wet weight of these altricial neonates is remarkably low, averaging just 3.2 grams [Wwb = 3.2 grams]. This minimal body mass at the moment of parturition is consistent with the pattern observed in small desert rodents, where the priority is to minimize the gestational burden on the female during a period when water and nutrient availability can be unpredictable. The gestation period itself, lasting approximately 29 days [tg = approximately 29 days] under the species' typical core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], is brief, allowing females to complete reproductive cycles rapidly when favorable conditions arise. This combination of a moderate litter size and a gestation of just under a month enables A. leucurus to capitalize on sporadic resource pulses characteristic of its desert habitat.

The nursing phase is relatively prolonged for an animal of this size, with the typical age at weaning recorded as 66 days after birth [tx = 66 days after birth] at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. When measured at a regulated body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the pup undergoes a dramatic increase in mass during this suckling period. At the point of nutritional independence and the cessation of lactation, the weanlings have typically attained a wet weight of 35 grams [Wwx = 35 grams]. This represents a more than tenfold increase over their birth weight, reflecting the high efficiency of the female's milk production in converting resources into offspring biomass. The pre-weaning developmental phase is a critical bottleneck for survival; pups that fail to maintain adequate growth rates are less likely to emerge from the natal burrow with sufficient fat reserves to withstand the thermal extremes of their desert habitat. This period of intense maternal investment places considerable physiological strain on the lactating female, who must forage extensively to meet the metabolic demands of her litter.

Sexual maturity in female White-tailed antelope squirrels typically occurs at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] under a core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This milestone is not reached until the second spring following their birth, meaning that a female born in early summer will not be reproductively active until the subsequent breeding season. The relatively late onset of puberty for a small rodent is somewhat unusual, but it reflects the species' bet-hedging strategy in an unpredictable environment; a female that delays reproduction ensures she has achieved full skeletal and fat reserve development before allocating energy to gestation and lactation. Field studies indicate that body mass is a stronger predictor of first estrus than chronological age, with females needing to surpass a minimum threshold of around 70 grams before their ovarian cycles are activated. Individuals that fail to achieve this mass prior to the breeding season must wait an additional year for their first opportunity to mate.

Extensive longitudinal studies have documented that the maximum lifespan attainable by this species in the wild is approximately 11.2 years [am = approximately 11.2 years] when measured at a core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This longevity is exceptionally high for a rodent of its size and is a hallmark of a slow life-history strategy, characterized by delayed maturity and relatively low annual fecundity. Such a long reproductive window allows females to accumulate multiple breeding attempts over their lifetime, which may partially compensate for the limitation of producing only approximately 1.3 litters each year. The physiological mechanisms underpinning this extended lifespan are thought to include a relatively high resistance to oxidative stress and a robust capacity for DNA repair, traits that are often correlated with the ability to maintain metabolic homeostasis in the face of the intense solar radiation and temperature fluctuations typical of their Mojave and Sonoran Desert environments. Annual survivorship of adults is high once they reach their prime years, with predation from raptors and rattlesnakes representing the primary sources of mortality.

The ultimate wet weight of a fully mature adult White-tailed antelope squirrel is typically reported as 105 grams [Wwi = 105 grams], a body size that places it at the upper end of the size range for its genus. Healthy, dominant individuals with access to high-quality territories replete with mesquite and yucca seeds routinely achieve this asymptotic mass (105 grams) [Wwi = 105 grams], which is roughly three times the weaning weight and represents a substantial post-weaning growth increment sustained by late-summer forb blooms. In comparative terms, the 105-gram adult mass is exceptional among North American ground squirrels of similar latitude, where many congeners peak below 90 grams. This body mass is achieved gradually over several months following weaning, and the ability to attain and maintain such a size is a strong determinant of overwinter survival and future reproductive success. During the winter torpor periods, individuals may lose a significant portion of their body fat, but healthy adults typically regain their full mass within weeks of emerging in late winter.
